sections.heading: The idea
sections.figure_alt: A curve of one variable, drawn on labeled axes.
sections.body_md:
A directional derivative asks how a scalar function changes when you leave a point along one chosen ray. Fix a point \(x\) and a direction \(d\). For a small positive number \(t\), the point \(x + t d\) lies on that ray. Subtract the old value from the new one and divide by \(t\). The directional derivative is the limit of those quotients as \(t\) decreases to 0.

The limit is one-sided on purpose. Negative \(t\) would walk the opposite ray. The slice \(g(t) = f(x + t d)\) is an ordinary function of one variable, and the directional derivative is the right-hand derivative of that slice at 0, when the right-hand derivative exists.

No gradient is required to ask the question. A corner in the slice can still have a right-hand slope. Scaling \(d\) by a positive number scales the derivative by the same number, because the parametrization got faster. At a corner the opposite ray can climb as well, so the derivative need not be linear in the direction. When a gradient exists and the function is differentiable, this slope agrees with the inner product of the gradient and the direction.

sections.heading: Key equations
sections.body_md:
The definition is the one-sided limit
\[
f'(x; d) = \lim_{t \downarrow 0} \frac{f(x + t d) - f(x)}{t},
\]
when the limit exists. If \(c > 0\) and both sides exist, then \(f'(x; c d) = c\, f'(x; d)\). Where \(f\) is differentiable,
\[
f'(x; d) = \nabla f(x)^{T} d.
\]
The right-hand side is linear in \(d\). The definition by itself does not promise that linearity.

sections.heading: Worked example
sections.body_md:
Take \(f(x, y) = 5x + y^2\) through (4, -1), and take the direction \((0, 2)\). The value at the point is \(20 + 1 = 21\). Along the ray the second coordinate is \(-1 + 2t\), so
\[
f(4,\ -1 + 2t) = 20 + ( -1 + 2t )^2 = 21 - 4t + 4t^2.
\]
The difference quotient is \(-4 + 4t\), and the limit is \(-4\). The first coordinate never moved, so the linear term \(5x\) contributed nothing to the slope. The factor 2 in the direction doubled the ordinary \(y\)-derivative, which is \(2y = -2\) at this point: \(2 \cdot (-2) = -4\).

sections.heading: Common pitfalls
sections.body_md: A two-sided limit is a stronger demand, and it is the wrong one for this definition. Dividing by the length of \(d\) answers a different question, the derivative in a unit direction. At a corner of an absolute value, both opposite directions can give a positive derivative, so you cannot recover one of them by negating the other. Reading the function value, or the sum of the direction's coordinates, does not produce a slope.

sections.heading: Where this leads
sections.body_md: Partial derivatives are the directional derivatives along the coordinate directions, and the gradient packages them so that every directional derivative is an inner product. Automatic differentiation in forward mode propagates exactly this directional derivative through a computation. A descent method later asks the inner product with the gradient to be negative, which is a sign restriction on this slope.
